/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.headline: Burnham says EU reset deal will add £17bn to UK economy
/politics/2026/nov/20/burnham-trade-yout.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham has taken the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals that ease trade and open a new mobility scheme for young people, as he declared a “new world” of cooperation between the two sides.

At a summit in Brussels on Friday, the EU and UK announced three deals: on food and drink, on emissions trading, and on a youth mobility scheme that will let 100,000 young Britons live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans coming to the UK.

The trio of deals could still be derailed within six months, however, as the EU has said it will block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

Burnham rejected suggestions there was any confusion over the deals coming into force: “The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” he said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”.

Hailing the “historic” agreement, Burnham said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe,” arguing that the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, economic growth, illegal immigration and the challenges facing young people.

The prime minister said he would “brainstorm” with the EU over future ties, while reiterating that he would not get ahead of public opinion.

Speaking to reporters, Burnham stressed that nothing would happen in the current parliament that went much beyond this deal. The so-called brainstorming process was, he said, “just looking at options in a new world, and having an open discussion about what those might be. It will be to inform the next parliament.”

Burnham also challenged political opponents, notably Nigel Farage, who held a retaliatory press conference in Brussels on Friday, to explain why they would reject a deal that he said would boost growth and lead to cheaper food and electricity. “Why would anybody turn their back on that?” he said.

The prime minister said the deals, which were initiated by Keir Starmer, would add 0.5% to British GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.

Farage said Burnham had been naive and that the EU had “used this moment to strongarm the British prime minister over tuition fee cuts for hundreds of thousands of EU students”.

EU leaders sought to play down the differences over tuition fees. “We are heading in the same direction and that is what matters,” the European Council president, António Costa, said of the broader relationship, describing the UK as “our closest neighbour, a reliable ally and a natural partner”.

Von der Leyen said it was up to the UK to decide where the journey was going, adding: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”

In a sign of tension in the negotiations, the EU agreed a declaration that the three deals would not come into force without equal treatment on fees for EU students at British universities.

“The [EU] Council and [European] Commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students,” stated the confidential statement seen by the Guardian. The EU would not adopt the three agreements before “the conclusions of the negotiations … providing for equal treatment on tuition fees”, it added.

Another potential flashpoint could be the UK’s status as a rule-taker. The food and drink and emissions trading deals require the UK to align with EU rules, and British experts will be invited to relevant EU meetings, including on potential animal health emergencies, though Britain will not have voting rights. Burnham rejected suggestions this was a fig leaf, saying it would be “quite a moment” to have British experts back in EU meeting rooms.

France was said to be instrumental in shaping Britain’s exclusion, although Paris argues its position was widely supported and reflects the reality that a non-member state cannot be a decision-maker.

After the talks, Burnham was treated to a lunch of pea and mint soup, battered North Sea cod and chips, followed by a Brussels waffle with fruit.

The summit began with a highly choreographed welcome ceremony in the Europa “space egg” European Council building, where a quintet played the British and EU anthems.

The UK hailed a joint decision to create a “partnership for economic resilience”, answering its concerns over the EU’s Made in Europe plans. The EU is still finalising legislation that would give EU companies preference when public money is spent on key technologies, such as renewables and electric cars, and the UK has been arguing for Britain to be included in Made in Europe so that UK firms are not locked out of European supply chains.

The two sides agreed to set up “a common prosperity and economic security space”, an answer to shared concerns about artificially cheap Chinese goods depressing prices across Europe, though questions over whether the UK needs to align with EU trade defences remain open. Burnham said the two sides had reached an agreement “to work together where we have common threats”.

In an echo of the Brexit years, the final deal emerged after late-night talks went to the wire.

The German Social Democrat MEP Bernd Lange called on both sides to resolve the tuition fees issue so studying stays affordable for young people, in a way that also works for universities: “We can’t open the door to young people and then price them out of walking through it.”

The EU has welcomed Burnham’s breaking of taboos over rejoining, though it also voiced frustration at British negotiating tactics. “The UK has a tendency to make even small questions so difficult,” an EU diplomat said. “A British prime minister talks about a change of approach … Then in negotiations it seems like British negotiators act the same way they always had.”

/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.headline: Livestreamed footage leads to 15-month jail term over Channel dinghy attack
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/far-right-activist-.bodyHtml:
The far-right agitator Daniel Thomas has been sentenced to 15 months in jail after slashing a dinghy that had been carrying asylum seekers in the Channel.

Judge Newton-Price KC said the offence amounted to a “flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption of the legitimate activities of the border force, the coastguard and RNLI [Royal National Lifeboat Institution] volunteers”, describing Thomas as a “publicity seeker” who had interfered with the work of law enforcement officers and lifesavers.

He added: “Those organisations perform essential roles in policing the maritime border. They do necessary, highly sensitive and very difficult jobs. Their work should not be interrupted by a publicity seeker slashing with a knife at a boat that they were trying to recover.”

Thomas, the founder of the anti-migration group Patriot Platform, had taken a boat out into the Channel and observed asylum seekers in a dinghy being assisted by the RNLI, Border Force and French coastguard on 22 September.

He asked for his boat to be steered towards the rigid-hulled inflatable boat, and armed himself with a knife as rescue crews approached the dinghy and a French man boarded it.

Newton-Price said Thomas had slashed the boat about eight times and that his actions would have alarmed anyone close at hand.

The judge said the fact the incident was livestreamed meant there must have been a “high degree of planning or premeditation”, with the video intended to be seen by a large audience on social media and replayed.

Thomas appeared from Winchester prison in Hampshire via video link. He made the sign of the cross at the start of the hearing and did not watch the livestream when it was shown in court. He slumped in his chair as the sentence was handed down.

Joel Smith KC, prosecuting, said aggravating features of the offence included that it took place on the “high seas” and while law enforcement officers were investigating potential immigration offences and RNLI volunteers were carrying out humanitarian work.

Smith said Thomas had five previous convictions, including public order offences, being carried in a stolen vehicle and fraud, and had been sentenced in 2016 to two years in jail for kidnap.

Simon Pentol KC, defending, described it as a “unique” case but said Thomas had not been charged with a racially motivated, terrorist or public order offence.

Pentol said: “The political element or landscape should be viewed though a very narrow prism.”

He told the court the incident began as “reportage” and the criminal damage was what Thomas had called a “spur of the moment opportunity”. Pentol said: “It was not premeditated. This was performative activism.” He added that the knife was not Thomas’s but was part of the boat’s equipment.

Pentol said Thomas had four children and was the sole provider for the family, and ran a successful business.

After slashing the dinghy with the knife, Thomas could be heard saying: “This is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats. Right, you’re on English territory. This is England; this is not France any more. Get off the boat; you have time to get off the boat. This is not France. Take them back.” He also said: “Traitors.”

The incident was captured on Thomas’s livestream, and the 37-year-old, also known as Danny Tommo, admitted criminal damage when he appeared at Portsmouth crown court via video link from prison.

After footage of the incident emerged, Thomas’s actions were condemned as violent and dangerous by the refugee charities Stand Up to Racism and the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants.

According to the RNLI, the rescued asylum seekers had been onboard the dinghy for 36 hours, thought to be the longest time small-boat passengers had spent crossing the Channel.

The RNLI said there had been concerns for their deteriorating health and fears of a “catastrophic failure” of the dinghy. The French coastguard said about 60 people on a small boat had spent more than 33 hours at sea “in precarious conditions” and refusing help as they were “determined to take all risks to reach the United Kingdom”.

/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.headline: AI-linked sell-off wipes trillions off global stock markets
/business/2026/nov/20/global-stock-marke.bodyHtml:
The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation of capital markets, and to reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies, as a global sell-off in AI-linked shares wiped trillions of dollars off markets worldwide.

The wider market dipped as Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading: on Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026, closing down 5% from its value on 1 January, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Nvidia shares also fell, after California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

/uk-news/2026/nov/20/sally-anne-bowen-po.headline: Police track down teacher who missed sentencing within hours
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/sally-anne-bowen-po.bodyHtml:
In an update on Friday afternoon, the Met said: “On Friday November 20, officers were made aware that a 65-year-old woman had failed to appear at Harrow crown court for sentencing.

“A warrant was issued for her arrest and officers promptly launched inquiries to locate her.

“At around 3pm, officers from a neighbouring force found the woman at a location in Hampshire and arrested her on suspicion of failing to appear at court.

“She has been taken into police custody. A new sentencing date will be set by the court in due course.”

Officers in Hampshire traced and arrested Bowen, a chemistry teacher who had sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s, hours after she failed to turn up to her sentencing hearing.

Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, could not be found at her home by Metropolitan police officers on Friday morning after a warrant was issued for her arrest, a court heard.

The former teacher, who was in her 20s when she had sex with one pupil up to 30 times and kissed a second boy when they were aged about 14 to 15, was convicted in August of seven counts of indecent assault and granted bail before her sentencing.

Her trial heard she wore short, tight skirts and flirted in class, with one former pupil comparing her behaviour to “a Sabrina Carpenter video”.

After her conviction she was granted bail and was due to be sentenced at Harrow crown court on Friday.

But Bowen, from Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, did not turn up to court in the morning, and the judge, Karim Ezzat, issued a warrant for her arrest, “not backed by bail”.

Neelam Gomersall, prosecuting, said Bowen’s partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, was at the address when officers arrived, but Bowen was not.

Gomersall had earlier told the court there was “no evidence” that Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and that information from Scotchbrook was “suggestive of refusal rather than inability” to attend.

Bowen’s barrister, Mark Kimsey, said: “Our instructing solicitor has tried to contact her and the phone rings but doesn’t answer.”

He had earlier said that Bowen was in contact with solicitors on Thursday and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been “concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages” from her.

Bowen’s trial heard that she was in her mid-20s when she taught at Christ’s College in Finchley, north London.

One victim had told jurors he had had sex with her “about 20 or 30 times” over several months, considered her his girlfriend and kept it secret. He said it had led to “the destruction of my education”.

The second victim described spending lunchtimes with Bowen in a cafe, where he was “goaded” into kissing her by other boys and recalled touching her breasts.

Bowen denied the allegations as “total fabrication” and claimed a medical condition made sex difficult and painful. She denied flirting, saying: “I didn’t flirt with students, I was just friendly.” Defending her clothes, she said she “wasn’t going to dress like Margaret Thatcher”.

/world/2026/nov/20/uk-france-veto-uae-ch.headline: Costa Rica's Grynspan remains frontrunner to become UN's first woman leader
/world/2026/nov/20/uk-france-veto-uae-ch.bodyHtml:
Rebeca Grynspan, the Costa Rican diplomat, remains the frontrunner to become the next UN secretary general. She collected 10 votes in Friday’s security council straw poll – enough to win the position outright – but needs no vote against her from any of the council’s five permanent members, the so-called P5: the US, UK, France, Russia and China. Two of them currently oppose her bid.

Should she win over the two permanent members believed to oppose her – thought to be the US and Russia – Grynspan would become the first woman to lead the UN.

The search for the world’s next chief diplomat remained deadlocked on Friday, after the UN security council’s ninth straw poll once again failed to settle on a winner.

At more than 100 days, the vote to replace the current secretary general, António Guterres, is already the longest in UN history – though another ballot is scheduled for next week, before his second term ends on 31 December.

The deadlock follows what is believed to be an effective veto, by the UK and France, of a controversial United Arab Emirates diplomat for the role, ostensibly over the UAE’s alleged links to atrocities in Sudan.

The Emirati diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, who had been a late entry into the race, received seven votes for but three against from the permanent members – a potentially insurmountable hurdle. Given her public support from the US and Russia, it appeared likely, according to multiple sources, that she was effectively vetoed by the UK, France and China.

Nearly 70 MPs had written to the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, arguing that Nusseibeh was not a “credible candidate” because she had “repeatedly denied and dismissed” reports by a UN panel of experts linking the UAE to atrocities in Sudan – part of widespread criticism of her candidacy.

UN panel reporting and rights groups have consistently said the UAE has hired mercenaries for, and provided weapons to, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the Sudanese paramilitary group the UN and US have determined has committed genocide in Darfur. The UAE denies involvement.

Nusseibeh has taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government, “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would require, she said, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

China’s opposition to Nusseibeh is grounded in its commitment to an unwritten convention that the secretary general’s position observes a geographic rotation, so all parts of the globe are ultimately represented: while the rotation principle has been ignored before, it is now the “turn” of Latin America or the Caribbean to hold the post.

Second on the latest ballot was Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, with eight “encourage” but three “discourage” votes from among the P5.

The process of electing the world’s chief diplomat is an arcane one, controlled by the security council, and dominated by the council’s five permanent members who wield an effective veto. Candidates need nine “encourage” votes from the 15 nations on the council: five permanent members (P5) and 10 elected members (E10). But the P5 carry an effective veto as a winning candidate must have the support of all five.

Elected members vote with white ballots, permanent members vote with red ballots. Voting is never disclosed but tallies are distributed through unofficial channels.

Daniel Safran-Hon, a senior adviser at the International Peace Institute who formerly worked in the UN secretary general’s executive office, said Grynspan was the “undisputed frontrunner”.

He said the Costa Rican, who is the head of the UN conference on trade and development (UNCTAD), needed to win over the remaining two P5 members resisting her candidacy.

“It is all speculation at this stage, but I would speculate that it’s not impossible. It’s not easy because the fact is that she’s been trying for a while to peel off American opposition, but she is the undisputed frontrunner: other candidates face a steeper hill.”

Grynspan has invoked her Jewish heritage to argue for the importance of ending conflict; her agency, UNCTAD, has exhaustively documented the economic damage wrought by Israel’s long-term occupation of the Palestinian territories. If elected, she would be the UN’s first Jewish secretary general.

She told the UN general assembly: “Peace is what made it possible for my parents, two refugees from the second world war, to find respect and dignity in a small country, Costa Rica. I am the daughter of this peace, a demonstration of what peace makes possible.”

/uk-news/2026/nov/20/friday-cold-weather.headline: Cold snap sparks surprise rebound in UK retail sales
/uk-news/2026/nov/20/friday-cold-weather.bodyHtml:
Retail sales overall made an unexpected recovery last month, the Office for National Statistics reported, confounding economists who had predicted a marginal decline of 0.1%.

Sales of clothing had increased at large supermarkets, it was reported on Friday, as more typical autumn weather boosted demand for autumn and winter lines after a warm September had held it back. Clothing and footwear stores reported 1.5% growth in sales volumes as a result.

Friday night will be the coldest night of the autumn so far, forecasters have said, surpassing the previous chilliest: Thursday.

A low of -8.4C was recorded at Tulloch Bridge in the Scottish Highlands overnight, according to the Met Office. Sub-zero temperatures were also recorded in Northern Ireland. More southerly areas stayed substantially warmer overnight on Thursday.

The Met Office said frost and rain, particularly present across northern parts of the UK in the morning, are largely expected to ease through the day on Friday, with some sunshine. But the frost will return fairly quickly as the sun sets, before another cold night.

“It will turn a lot colder as we head through into the weekend,” said meteorologist Clare Nasir.

“Through this evening and overnight, any residual spits and spots of rain will tend to clear as we see starry skies evolve and that frost extends southwards through the night.

“It will be severe in the north, so we could see temperatures as low as around -8C, -9C in one or two glens. And, farther south, we’re expecting some sub-zero temperatures. A cold end tonight, even some freeze and fog patches, particularly across central, southern areas and in Northern Ireland.”

For most, Saturday is forecast to be dry with some sunshine. It follows the first snow warning of the season, with more than an inch recorded in parts of northern England on Tuesday.

A yellow cold health alert is in force for the north-west, the north-east and Yorkshire and the Humber until 9am on Monday. The alerts mean weather conditions could result in an increased use of healthcare services and a greater risk to life for vulnerable people, according to the UK Health Security Agency. Yellow alerts indicate a moderate likelihood and level of impact.

There are 12 flood alerts in place for England, indicating flooding is possible, after a spell of wet weather.

/film/2026/nov/20/gerard-depardieu-miche.headline: Woman's complaint leads French police to investigate Depardieu and Houellebecq
/film/2026/nov/20/gerard-depardieu-miche.bodyHtml:
French police are investigating allegations that the actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq gang-raped and assaulted a woman during a 2018 film shoot.

The investigative website Mediapart reported this week that an actor, given the pseudonym Alexandra, had made a complaint to police in 2025.

Two sources following the case confirmed to Agence France-Presse on Friday that a police investigation was under way.

The alleged attack took place in December 2018 during the shooting of Thalasso, a film starring the two men as versions of themselves who meet at a health spa and have long philosophical conversations while in white bath-robes.

Alexandra, an eastern European actor and dancer who was 32 at the time and working in France, told Mediapart that she was attacked by Depardieu and Houellebecq as they pinned her down during one scene and while cameras filmed.

Mediapart reported that Alexandra described being “in a state of stupefaction and disconnect”. In her police complaint she had spoken of “deep humiliation” and “indescribable shame”.

The film’s director, Guillaume Nicloux, had been accused of complicity in the sexual abuse, AFP reported.

Nicloux told Mediapart that at the moment of filming he had not “noticed any constraint”, but he had “apologised” to Alexandra.

Alexandra’s lawyers did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. Depardieu’s lawyers did not respond to a request for comment. The Guardian contacted Houellebecq’s publishers, who did not respond.

This week Depardieu, 77, dropped his appeal against a 2025 conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a different film set in 2021, and apologised to them.

At his trial last year, Depardieu was found guilty of sexually assaulting a 55-year-old set dresser and a 35-year-old assistant director during the shooting of the feature film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters) in Paris in September 2021. His suspended sentence will now stand and his name has been added to France’s sex offender register.

After Depardieu’s apology this week, the assistant director whom he sexually assaulted said: “The monster of cinema has fallen.”

Depardieu’s conviction last year was a turning point for the #MeToo movement in France. He became the biggest figure in the French film industry to be convicted of sexual assault after years of criticism of the country’s reluctance to take women’s claims of abuse seriously.

He has appealed against a separate decision requiring him to face trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting the actor Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in 2018. Appeal judges will rule this month on whether to uphold his appeal or allow the trial to go ahead next year.

In an open letter to Le Figaro in October 2023, Depardieu denied all allegations and said any encounter with Arnould had been consensual. “Never, ever, have I abused a woman,” he wrote.

Houellebecq, 70, who is among France’s most translated authors, is also under investigation for alleged incitement to discrimination in France over comments he made in 2022 about Muslims.

  • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.headline: Bayern Munich rally around Kane as club doctors weigh up surgery
/football/2026/nov/20/harry-kane-ankle-l.bodyHtml:
Bayern Munich’s medical team are already weighing up treatment options for Harry Kane, who will be “out for the next few months” after tearing a ligament in his left ankle during Friday’s 1-1 draw with Cologne.

Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied. The returning Bayern coach, Vincent Kompany, said the injury would take “months” rather than weeks to heal.

A club statement on X said: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”

The Bayern sporting director, Max Eberl, said on Friday that club doctors were “discussing whether or not to recommend surgery” for Kane’s injury, as the 33-year-old may face a race to be fit for the Nations League quarter-finals, the first leg of which takes place in Norway on 27 March – just over four months away.

Part of Kane’s recovery period will come during the Bundesliga’s winter break from 20 December to 8 January. He will, however, miss Champions League games away to Lille next week and at home to Slavia Prague next month, as well as the January trip to Manchester United and the league phase finale at home to Real Betis.

“I think this result was fair and Cologne deserved the point,” Kompany said after the game. “We have other worries now, I have to honestly say. We will all try together to make something strong out of this situation. FC Bayern does that time and again, and that’s what we want to do now too.”

The Tottenham loanee Mikey Moore fired the visitors ahead before Kane’s injury, but Bayern levelled when Nathaniel Brown scored before the break. Bayern also lost Michael Olise to injury for the second half, and Said El Mala missed an excellent late chance to earn Cologne’s first win at Bayern since 2009.

Kane’s setback adds to an extensive Bayern injury list, with Olise also going off during Friday’s game with a foot contusion. Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and Manuel Neuer were already unavailable, leaving Kompany short of options for a busy month of fixtures.

Kompany returned from his own month-long absence for Friday’s game with his arm in a sling, having dislocated his shoulder when he collapsed on a training pitch in October. The Belgian was taken to hospital for meningeal irritation treatment after his collapse, and has been recovering at home.

Cologne took a surprise lead with 12 minutes gone when Moore started and finished an excellent break. The teenage winger pounced on a mislaid Olise pass and drove forward, finding Linton Maina who laid off for El Mala, whose no-look backheel pass allowed Moore to round keeper Jonas Urbig before sliding the ball home.

Kane was then brought down in the Cologne box from behind by Schmied, who got the ball first but clattered into Kane’s left leg in his follow-through. Kane’s penalty appeals were waved away, but he was left visibly limping and received treatment on his ankle before being replaced by Tom Bischof on the 20-minute mark.

The hosts levelled 17 minutes later when full-back Brown sliced a low shot into the bottom-right corner, but suffered another blow just before the break when Olise went down. The France star did not return for the second half and was seen leaving the stadium shortly after on crutches – but it appears unlikely he will miss a significant amount of time.

Just before the hour mark, El Mala and Maina forced a spectacular double save from Urbig. El Mala, recently called up by Germany, then had a golden chance to put Cologne in front with eight minutes to go when one-on-one with Urbig – but he cut his close-range shot inches wide of the post.

Now a point behind Bayern, Borussia Dortmund can move into outright first place if they win at bottom club Mönchengladbach on Saturday. Freiburg can also move level on points with Bayern if they can defeat promoted Elversberg.

This month Kane signed a new deal with the Bundesliga giants until June 2029, which is reportedly worth in excess of £400,000 a week, making him the highest-paid player in Europe before bonuses.

Since arriving from Tottenham three years ago, Kane has scored 156 goals in 163 appearances, helping Bayern win a league and cup double last season.
